Canada's Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program—administered jointly by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) and the Department of Finance Canada under the federal Income Tax Act (R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) and Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945)—has undergone its most consequential legislative expansion in over a decade. Following proposals introduced in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement and expanded in the November 4, 2025 federal budget (Budget 2025), Parliament enacted Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Retroactive to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the legislation doubles the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 (increasing the maximum annual enhanced refundable credit from $1,050,000 to $2,100,000), widens the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, introduces an elective three-year average gross revenue phase-out alternative for Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs), and extends the 35% enhanced refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) for the first time. Concurrently, for depreciable property acquired (and lease costs first becoming payable) after December 15, 2024, the legislation restores the eligibility of SR&ED capital expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and equipment lease expenditures, reversing the 2014 repeal of capital eligibility.

At the sub-national level, the provincial response to the federal Bill C-15 reforms has bifurcated into followers, independent holdouts, and structural reformers. British Columbia expressly aligned its 10% refundable SR&ED tax credit with the federal $6,000,000 expenditure limit, $15 million–$75 million phase-out thresholds, ECPC eligibility, and capital expenditure restoration, while removing its credit expiry date in BC Budget 2026 to make the provincial credit permanent. Quebec executed a sweeping structural consolidation for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, abolishing eight legacy R&D tax credits (including the legacy Form RD-1029.7 salary credit) and replacing them with the unified Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), which provides a 100% refundable 30% credit on the first $1,000,000 of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures above an exclusion floor and 20% on the excess, inclusive of capital equipment. Conversely, Ontario (8% refundable OITC capped at $3,000,000; 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC; 20% refundable OBRITC) and Alberta (8% base and 20% incremental refundable Innovation Employment Grant capped at $4,000,000) have retained their distinct provincial architectures without adopting the $6,000,000 federal expenditure limit.
1. Executive Summary and the 2024–2026 Federal SR&ED Legislative Overhaul
1.1 Evolution from the 2024 Fall Economic Statement to Budget 2025 and Bill C-15

The statutory modernization of the federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) program unfolded in two distinct policy stages between December 2024 and March 2026. In the federal 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES), tabled on December 16, 2024 (followed by draft legislative proposals released by the Department of Finance Canada on August 15, 2025), the federal government initially proposed raising the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3,000,000 to $4,500,000, expanding the taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extending the enhanced 35% credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a consolidated gross revenue phase-out test, and restoring the eligibility of SR&ED capital expenditures and lease costs after an eleven-year hiatus.

On November 4, 2025, the Minister of Finance and National Revenue, François-Philippe Champagne, presented Budget 2025, which superseded the $4,500,000 interim proposal by doubling the annual enhanced expenditure limit directly from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000, retroactive to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. These legislative amendments were codified in Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Following Royal Assent, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) launched an elective Pre-Claim Approval process on April 1, 2026, released revised Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim), Form T1145, and Form T1146 on May 15, 2026, published updated T2 Schedule 31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations) on May 22, 2026 and T2 Schedule 49 on May 29, 2026 (further updated October 19, 2026), and issued updated administrative policies between May and October 2026.

body.text: 1.3 Transitional Application Rules for Non-Calendar Taxation Years and Capital Property

Because the legislative amendments enacted in Bill C-15 apply through two distinct statutory effective triggers, taxpayers and auditors must distinguish between taxation-year-based measures and acquisition-date-based measures:

items: Taxation-Year Trigger (Enhanced $6M Limit, $15M–$75M Phase-Out, and ECPC Access): The doubling of the expenditure limit to $6,000,000, the expanded $15 million to $75 million phase-out range, the CCPC gross revenue election, and the eligibility of Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) apply strictly to taxation years that begin after December 15, 2024. Corporations with calendar taxation years first benefit from these enhancements in the taxation year beginning January 1, 2025. Conversely, as tax advisory guidance highlights, a corporation with a June 30 fiscal year-end does not qualify for the $6,000,000 limit or ECPC access for its taxation year running from July 1, 2024 to June 30, 2025 (which remains subject to the $3,000,000 limit and $10 million–$50 million phase-out), and first enters the expanded regime for its taxation year beginning July 1, 2025. Because Bill C-15 received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, corporations whose qualifying taxation years began after December 15, 2024 and ended in 2025 or early 2026—and that filed under pre-change administrative practices—may amend their claims to capture the higher limits and capital costs, provided the amendment is submitted within the statutory 18-month reporting deadline from the end of the taxation year.

Transaction-Date Trigger (Capital Expenditures, SUE, and Lease Costs): The restoration of SR&ED capital expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and equipment lease costs applies to depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 (i.e., on or after December 16, 2024), and, in the case of lease expenditures, amounts that first become payable after December 15, 2024. If a claimant's taxation year straddles December 15, 2024 (meaning the taxation year began before December 16, 2024 and ended on or after December 16, 2024), capital property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 is eligible in that straddle year, and the percentage of SR&ED operating time for leased equipment in that transition year is calculated specifically over the period after December 15, 2024. Capital expenditures or lease payments incurred before December 16, 2024 remain permanently ineligible for SR&ED tax incentives.

body.text: 2. Statutory and Regulatory Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Program
2.1 Dual-Incentive Mechanism: Section 37 Expenditure Pool and Section 127 Investment Tax Credits
The federal SR&ED program operates under a two-stage statutory architecture within the Income Tax Act (ITA):

items: First Stage — The Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures (ITA s. 37(1)): A taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada may accumulate allowable current SR&ED expenditures (paragraph 37(1)(a)) and, for property acquired after December 15, 2024, allowable capital SR&ED expenditures (paragraph 37(1)(b)) in a cumulative tax pool. Unlike ordinary business expenses under section 9 or capital cost allowance (CCA) under paragraph 20(1)(a), the Section 37 pool allows the taxpayer to deduct up to 100% of the available pool balance against business income in the current taxation year or defer any portion of the deduction to future taxation years. A positive balance in the Section 37 pool does not expire and may be carried forward indefinitely as a running balance.

Second Stage — The Section 127 & 127.1 Investment Tax Credit (ITA s. 127(5), s. 127(9), s. 127(10.1), s. 127.1): Based on the claimant's annual "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" (subsection 127(9)), which starts from allowable expenditures on Form T661 and incorporates specific statutory additions (such as the Prescribed Proxy Amount and Shared-Use Equipment) and reductions (such as the 20% exclusion on arm's-length contracts and third-party payments, prescribed expenditures under Regulation 2902, and government/non-government assistance), the claimant earns an Investment Tax Credit (ITC). Earned ITCs must first be applied to reduce Part I federal income tax otherwise payable to nil in the current taxation year (subsection 127(5)). Depending on the claimant's legal status and expenditure type, unused current-year ITCs may then be refunded in cash (section 127.1), carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years, or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years.

body.text: 2.3 Mechanics of the Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures

Under subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act, the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures functions as a perpetual running account computed at the end of each taxation year on Part 3, Section C (Lines 420 to 470) of Form T661. Unlike capital cost allowance (CCA) pools, the Section 37 pool is not segregated by asset class or vintage year.
Increases to the Section 37 Pool

The pool balance at the end of a taxation year is increased by six statutory additions. First, under paragraph 37(1)(a), the taxpayer adds allowable expenditures of a current nature on SR&ED carried on in Canada directly undertaken by or on behalf of the claimant, including directly engaged or directly attributable salaries and wages, materials consumed or transformed, lease costs of equipment incurred after December 15, 2024, 100% of arm's-length and non-arm's length SR&ED contracts, eligible third-party payments, and directly related and incremental overhead under the Traditional Method. Second, under paragraph 37(1)(b), the taxpayer adds allowable expenditures of a capital nature made after December 15, 2024 to acquire new or used depreciable property (excluding buildings and leasehold interests in buildings) that becomes available for use in the year and meets the All or Substantially All (ASA ≥ 90%) operating-time or value-consumed intent test. Third, under paragraph 37(1)(c), the pool is increased by amounts of government or non-government assistance repaid by the taxpayer in the year, to the extent those amounts previously reduced the Section 37 pool under paragraph 37(1)(d). Fourth, under paragraph 37(1)(c.1), the taxpayer adds any negative Section 37 pool balance that was required to be included in the taxpayer's income in a preceding taxation year pursuant to paragraph 12(1)(v). Fifth, under paragraphs 37(1)(c.2) and 37(1)(c.3), the taxpayer adds amounts included in Part I tax payable in the immediately preceding taxation year due to the recapture of an SR&ED ITC (subsections 127(27) to 127(30)) or a partnership ITC recapture excess amount. Sixth, undeducted Section 37 pool balances are inherited from predecessor corporations on a qualifying amalgamation (subsection 87(2)(l)) or wind-up of a subsidiary (subsection 88(1)(e.2)).
Decreases to the Section 37 Pool and Negative Pool Balances

From the cumulative additions, the taxpayer must subtract five statutory reductions. First, under paragraph 37(1)(d), the pool is reduced by all government assistance (including provincial/territorial R&D tax credits, NRC-IRAP grants, and forgivable loans, but excluding the federal SR&ED ITC itself) and non-government assistance that the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive at the filing-due date in respect of SR&ED expenditures claimed in the pool (reported on Lines 429, 431, and 432 of Form T661); however, contract payments received by an SR&ED performer reduce qualified expenditures for ITC purposes under subsection 127(9) and do not reduce the performer's Section 37 deductible expenditure pool. Second, under paragraph 37(1)(d.1), any provincial super-allowance benefit amounts are deducted. Third, under paragraph 37(1)(e), the pool is reduced by federal SR&ED ITCs claimed as a deduction against Part I tax payable or received as a cash refund in the immediately preceding taxation year (other than ITCs allocated from a partnership, which reduce the partnership's pool in the subsequent year under subsection 127(12.1)). Fourth, under paragraphs 37(1)(f) and 37(1)(f.1), the pool is reduced by optional deductions claimed in computing income in preceding taxation years (37(1)(f)) and insolvency deductions claimed under section 61.3 in preceding years (37(1)(f.1)). Fifth, under paragraph 37(1)(h), the pool is reduced by amounts determined under subsection 37(6.1) upon a loss restriction event (acquisition of control).

If the mandatory reductions—most commonly the prior-year federal ITC deduction or refund under paragraph 37(1)(e) when the taxpayer claimed the Prescribed Proxy Amount (which generates an ITC without ever entering the Section 37 pool) and deducted the entire Section 37 pool in the prior year—cause the Section 37 pool balance at the end of the taxation year to become negative, that negative balance must be included in the taxpayer's business income for the year under paragraph 12(1)(v), and the pool balance is restored to nil in the subsequent year via paragraph 37(1)(c.1).
Prohibition on Acquisition of Rights (Subsection 37(4)) and Loss Restriction Events (Subsection 37(6.1))

Under subsection 37(4) of the ITA (and paragraph 2902(c) of the ITR), no deduction or ITC is permitted for any expenditure made to acquire rights in, or arising out of, SR&ED (such as purchasing patents, technology licences, or completed R&D intellectual property from another entity). The CRA enforces this prohibition to prevent duplication of tax incentives (as the original performer was entitled to claim the SR&ED) and to prevent foreign R&D from entering the Canadian incentive system through IP acquisitions.

When a corporation undergoes an acquisition of control (a "loss restriction event"), a deemed taxation year-end occurs immediately prior to the acquisition, and the corporation's undeducted Section 37 pool balance is reduced to nil (paragraph 37(1)(h) and subsection 37(6.1)). In post-acquisition taxation years, the pre-acquisition Section 37 pool may be reinstated and deducted only if (1) the specific business to which the SR&ED expenditures related continues to be carried on by the corporation for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit throughout the subsequent year, and (2) only to the extent of the corporation's income for that subsequent year from that same business or a similar business. Similar streaming restrictions apply to unused Section 127 ITC carryforwards and carrybacks upon an acquisition of control.
3. Federal Investment Tax Credit Rates, Expenditure Limits, Phase-Out Mechanics, and Refundability
3.1 Qualifying CCPCs vs. Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)

Prior to the Bill C-15 reforms, only a Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC)—a private Canadian corporation not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever (de jure or de facto control), by one or more non-resident persons, by one or more public corporations, or by any combination thereof—could access the enhanced 35% SR&ED ITC rate. Previously, if a CCPC completed an initial public offering (IPO) on a designated stock exchange, it immediately lost access to the 35% refundable rate and dropped to the 15% non-refundable rate.

For taxation years that begin after December 15, 2024, subsections 127(9) and 127(10.1) extend the enhanced 35% SR&ED ITC rate and the $6,000,000 annual expenditure limit to an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC). Under the statutory definition in subsection 127(9), a corporation qualifies as an ECPC throughout a taxation year if it satisfies all four of the following criteria:

items: Canadian Residency: It is resident in Canada throughout the taxation year;
Public Listing or Designation: It has a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange, or it has elected (or been designated by the Minister of National Revenue) to be a public corporation;
Absence of Non-Resident Control: It is not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons; and

Deemed Control Test: It would not be controlled by a particular person if all shares of the corporation owned by non-resident persons were owned by that person (determined on the basis of publicly available information).

body.text: Furthermore, a Canadian-resident subsidiary corporation that is not itself listed on a stock exchange also qualifies under the ECPC rules if all or substantially all (90% or more) of its shares are owned, directly or indirectly, by one or more ECPCs throughout the taxation year.
3.2 Mathematical Phase-Out Formulas: Taxable Capital vs. Consolidated Gross Revenue

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the maximum annual expenditure limit is $6,000,000, which must be shared among all associated corporations (T2 Schedule 49) or members of a consolidated corporate group. To illustrate the strategic benefit of the CCPC election, consider a venture-backed Canadian CCPC whose fiscal year begins January 1, 2025, with prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of $45,000,000 and three-year average gross revenue of $8,000,000. Under the default Taxable Capital Method, its excess taxable capital over $15,000,000 is $30,000,000 ($45,000,000 minus $15,000,000), which reduces its expenditure limit by $3,000,000 (0.10 × $30,000,000) to $3,000,000. By electing the Gross Revenue Method, because its three-year average gross revenue ($8,000,000) is below the $15,000,000 threshold, the reduction is $0, and the CCPC preserves its full $6,000,000 expenditure limit—unlocking an additional $600,000 ($3,000,000 × 20% rate differential) in enhanced refundable SR&ED tax credits.

body.text: Multi-Tier Calculation Example (Qualifying CCPC with $8,000,000 in Current Qualified Expenditures)
Suppose a qualifying CCPC with a full $6,000,000 expenditure limit incurs $8,000,000 of qualified current SR&ED expenditures in its 2025 calendar taxation year and has $0 Part I tax payable:

items: First $6,000,000 (Enhanced Tier): Earns 35% × $6,000,000 = $2,100,000 ITC. Because these are current expenditures within the expenditure limit, 100% is refundable in cash = $2,100,000.

Remaining $2,000,000 (Basic Tier above Limit): Earns 15% × $2,000,000 = $300,000 ITC. Because the corporation is a qualifying CCPC, 40% of the 15% basic ITC is refundable in cash = 40% × $300,000 = $120,000, while the remaining $180,000 is a non-refundable ITC that may be carried back 3 years or carried forward 20 years.
Total Current-Year Cash Refund: $2,100,000 + $120,000 = $2,220,000 (plus $180,000 non-refundable ITC carryforward).

body.text: 3.4 Special Entity Rules: Partnerships, Joint Ventures, Individuals, and Trusts

Although a partnership is not a separate legal person or taxpayer under the Income Tax Act, paragraph 96(1)(a) requires the partnership to compute its net income or loss as if it were a separate person. Under the CRA's SR&ED Claims for Partnerships Policy, five strict statutory rules govern SR&ED conducted by a partnership:

items: Mandatory Full Pool Deduction (No Carryforward): Unlike corporations or individuals, a partnership cannot carry forward any balance in its Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures to a subsequent fiscal period. The entire Section 37 pool must be deducted in full in computing the partnership's net business income or loss for the fiscal period in which the expenditures were incurred.

Exclusion from the Enhanced 35% Rate: Under subsection 127(8), the SR&ED ITC of a partnership is calculated exclusively at the 15% basic rate and allocated to its members according to their reasonable share. As confirmed by the courts in All Colour Chemicals, even if all partners of a partnership are qualifying CCPCs, the partnership-allocated ITC is restricted to 15% because subsection 127(8) overrides subsection 127(10.1). Furthermore, the allocation of an SR&ED ITC from a partnership reduces the partnership's Section 37 pool in the subsequent tax year under subsection 127(12.1).

Ineligibility of Partner Salaries: A partner cannot be an employee of the partnership for income tax purposes; consequently, any salary or drawings paid to a partner is treated as a distribution of partnership income and cannot be claimed as SR&ED salary or wages.

No Non-Arm's Length Transfers (Subsection 127(13)): Because subsection 127(13) applies only between "taxpayers" and a partnership is not a taxpayer, qualified SR&ED expenditures cannot be transferred via Form T1146 between a partnership and a non-arm's length taxpayer.

Restrictions on Limited Partners and Specified Members (Subsections 96(2.4), 127(8), 127(8.3)–(8.4), and 248(1)): A limited partner (subsection 96(2.4)) or a specified member (subsection 248(1)—any limited partner, plus any general partner who was not regularly, continuously, and substantially actively engaged in the partnership's business activities other than financing, or carrying on a similar business, during the tax year) is subject to strict limitations. Partnership losses created or increased by claiming the Section 37 pool are restricted for limited partners to their "at-risk amount," and ITCs allocated because of a specified member may be renounced by election under subsections 127(8.3) and 127(8.4) so that the extinguished ITCs do not reduce the partnership's Section 37 pool. By contrast, participants in an unincorporated joint venture file their own separate SR&ED claims directly for the work they performed or funded.

body.text: 4. Scientific and Technological Eligibility Framework: Subsection 248(1) and Administrative Guidelines
4.1 Statutory Definition of SR&ED under Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act

The foundational legal test for what work qualifies as SR&ED is codified in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. Under subsection 248(1), "scientific research and experimental development" means a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis and that is:

items: Paragraph 248(1)(a) — Basic Research: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view.
Paragraph 248(1)(b) — Applied Research: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view.

Paragraph 248(1)(c) — Experimental Development: Work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Across all Canadian SR&ED claims, experimental development accounts for the vast majority of corporate filings; according to CRA annual program statistics cited in industry analyses, software development alone accounted for 42.6% of all ITCs allowed in 2025–2026 (up from 35.7% in 2021–2022), while 59% of all ITCs allowed in 2025–2026 were refundable and 41% non-refundable.

body.text: Eligible Support Work (Paragraph 248(1)(d)) and Statutory Exclusions (Paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k))

Under paragraph 248(1)(d), SR&ED includes work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to eight specific disciplines—(1) engineering, (2) design, (3) operations research, (4) mathematical analysis, (5) computer programming, (6) data collection, (7) testing, or (8) psychological research—where the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research (a), applied research (b), or experimental development (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. (Note: On June 26, 2013, royal assent was received to amend paragraph 248(1)(d) of the French version of the Act, replacing "travaux techniques" with "travaux de génie" to align with "engineering" in the English text.)

Conversely, paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) explicitly exclude from SR&ED any work with respect to: (e) market research or sales promotion; (f) quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; (g) research in the social sciences or the humanities; (h) prospecting, exploring or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; (i) the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; (j) style changes; or (k) routine data collection.
4.2 The Common-Law Five Questions (Northwest Hydraulic) vs. The CRA's "Why and How" Framework

For over two decades, both the Tax Court of Canada and the CRA evaluated SR&ED eligibility through the five criteria articulated by Justice Donald Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen (98 DTC 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (TCC)). In the CRA's former Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (published December 19, 2012, revised April 24, 2015, and archived August 13, 2021), those judicial criteria were expressed as five sequential questions: (1) Was there a scientific or a technological uncertainty? (2) Did the effort involve formulating hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty? (3) Was the overall approach adopted consistent with a systematic investigation or search, including formulating and testing the hypotheses by means of experiment or analysis? (4) Was the overall approach undertaken for the purpose of achieving a scientific or a technological advancement? and (5) Was a record of the hypotheses tested and the results kept as the work progressed?.

On August 13, 2021 (updated July 5, 2022), the CRA replaced the archived 2015 policy with the Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentives, consolidating the analytical framework into Two Requirements: The "Why" Requirement and The "How" Requirement. Crucially, as confirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada (2021 FCA 88) and National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72), both the Five Questions and the Two Requirements derive from the unchanged text of subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, and the CRA's 2021 guidelines did not relax or eliminate the common-law Northwest Hydraulic requirement that the taxpayer's work adhere to the scientific method.

body.text: 4.3 Production Runs (ED+EP vs. ED+CP) and Developing Commercial Assets
1. SR&ED During Production Runs Policy (ED+EP vs. ED+CP)

When experimental development (ED) is performed during a manufacturing production run, the CRA's SR&ED During Production Runs Policy (updated July 19, 2016) classifies the run into one of two contexts, with ED+CP serving as the default classification unless the claimant establishes ED+EP:

items: Experimental Development with Experimental Production (ED+EP): Occurs where there is experimental development and the resulting output is experimental production (EP) required to verify whether the objectives of the SR&ED work have been met or if a technological advancement is achievable, with no simultaneous commercial work occurring. To establish ED+EP, there must be a technical risk to the process or product attributable to technological uncertainties arising from testing process parameters outside normal established processes, procedures, ranges, and tolerances—such as uncertainty over how the experiment will impact the process or product, risk that the process becomes unstable (causing output inconsistencies, production interruptions, stoppages, or equipment damage), or uncertain efficiency causing abnormal yield losses. Under ED+EP, the full cost of labour and materials consumed or transformed during the experimental run is allowable, excluding any excess production beyond what is required to evaluate the SR&ED and excluding input material costs incurred in commercial production steps prior to the step where experimental development began. Subsequent sale of the output does not alter the ED+EP classification, though selling transformed materials triggers ITC recapture under subsection 127(27).

Experimental Development with Commercial Production (ED+CP): Occurs where experimental development is conducted in conjunction or simultaneously with commercial production. Under ED+CP, all normal commercial production costs (standard labour, standard input materials, normal scrap/yield loss, and ramp-up/ramp-down outside the experimental phase) are strictly excluded, leaving only the additional (incremental) costs of labour, overhead, and materials consumed or transformed (such as actual loss of materials minus standard loss of materials) as allowable. Where it is impossible to isolate SR&ED work in an ED+CP run, the CRA permits an alternative Incremental Cost Method (actual costs incurred for the ED+CP run minus standard production costs attributable to commercial production without ED), provided the CRA agrees and the claimant signs a formal waiver of the right to object or appeal under subsection 169(2.2) of the Income Tax Act.

body.text: 2. SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy (Custom Products, Commercial Assets, and Pilot Plants)

Under the CRA's SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy (updated July 19, 2016), when a taxpayer develops a custom product, a commercial asset, or a pilot plant, the claimant must identify the specific components constructed and allocate project costs between SR&ED work and commercial non-SR&ED work. Allowable current expenditures (salary or wages, overhead, SR&ED contracts, and materials consumed or transformed) incurred to resolve technological uncertainties on eligible components retain their current nature. However, the CRA does not allow the practice of claiming all materials transformed in a custom product or commercial asset and relying on subsequent ITC recapture; no material costs are allowed for portions of the asset that did not involve SR&ED, even if they are an integral part of the commercial asset.
5. Qualifying SR&ED Expenditures, Calculation Methods, and Restoration of Capital and Lease Costs
5.1 Election Between the Proxy Method and Traditional Method (Subsection 37(10))

Every SR&ED claimant must select either the Proxy Method (ITA clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)) or the Traditional Method (ITA clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)) on Lines 160 and 162 of Part 3 of Form T661 for each taxation year. Under subsection 37(10) of the Income Tax Act, the election is made annually for each taxation year. If a claimant does not select a method on Form T661, the CRA processes the claim using the Traditional Method.

body.text: 5.2 Salary or Wages, Specified Employee Caps, and the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)
1. Directly Engaged vs. Directly Undertaking, Supervising, or Supporting

Under subsection 248(1), "salary or wages" means employment income computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the ITA (sections 5 to 8), excluding superannuation or pension benefits and retiring allowances. Under the Proxy Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)), only the portion of salary or wages of employees directly engaged in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada is allowable. Whether an employee is "directly engaged" depends strictly on the hands-on tasks performed, not the employee's job title. Directly engaged tasks include preparing equipment and materials for experiments, carrying out experiments and analysis, recording measurements, technological planning for ongoing SR&ED projects claimed in the tax year (such as planning for assignment of technological personnel, job priorities, development of technological strategies, and quality of materials used), and certain tasks performed by non-specialized employees (such as operating a machine required for an experiment or feeding raw materials into a machine) when supervised by staff with scientific or technological qualifications.

Under both the Traditional and Proxy methods, where All or Substantially All (ASA — 90% or more) of an employee's salary or wages is attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, 100% of the expenditure is deemed to be attributable to SR&ED (ITR subsection 2900(5)).
2. Specified Employees: Definition and Dual Statutory Caps (5 × YMPE and 2.5 × YMPE)

Under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, a specified employee is an employee who either (1) is a specified shareholder of the employer (a person who owns, directly or indirectly, at any time during the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the capital stock of the employer or of any corporation related to the employer, including shares owned by persons with whom the employee does not deal at arm's length under section 251), OR (2) does not deal at arm's length with the employer (such as a spouse, brother, or sister of a controlling shareholder).
Specified employees are subject to three strict statutory restrictions across two levels of the SR&ED calculation:

items: Complete Exclusion of Bonuses and Profit-Based Remuneration (ITA Subsection 37(9)): Unlike regular arm's-length employees (whose bonuses and profit-based remuneration are allowable in the Section 37 pool, though excluded from the PPA salary base), any bonus or remuneration based on profits paid to a specified employee is completely excluded from allowable SR&ED expenditures. Furthermore, dividends paid to founder-shareholders do not constitute employment salary or wages and add nothing to the SR&ED claim or salary base.

Allowable SR&ED Expenditure Ceiling — 5 × YMPE (ITA Subsection 37(9.1)): The maximum amount of salary or wages of a specified employee that can be claimed as an allowable SR&ED expenditure in Part 3 of Form T661 is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the claimant's taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year on which the individual is a specified employee: Maximum allowable salary or wages = A × B ÷ 365, where A is 5 × YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends and B is the number of days in the taxation year on which the employee is a specified employee of the claimant. If a specified employee performs SR&ED for two or more associated corporations, no amount may be claimed unless the associated corporations file an agreement on Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for SR&ED) under subsections 37(9.3) and 37(9.4) allocating the 5 × YMPE ceiling among the group.

PPA Salary Base Ceiling — Lesser of 75% of Total Salary or 2.5 × YMPE (ITR Subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8)): When computing the Salary Base in Part 5 of Form T661 (Lines 850 to 860) to calculate the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount, the amount included for each specified employee is restricted to the lesser of:

75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages (both SR&ED and non-SR&ED) for the year, excluding bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year; OR

2.5 × YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days the claimant employed the individual in the taxation year (with no proration for days the employee was not a specified employee): Salary base limit = 2.5 × A × (B ÷ 365), where A is the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends and B is the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual. Across associated corporations (and deemed associated entities under ITR subsection 2900(10)), the aggregate amount included in the PPA salary base for a specified employee cannot exceed 2.5 × YMPE (ITR subsection 2900(8)).

body.text: 3. Calculation of the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) and Overall Cap (ITR 2900(4)–(9))

Under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is equal to 55% of the Salary Base (Line 818 × 55% = Line 820 of Form T661). Under ITR subsection 2900(9), for any employee (whether specified or non-specified), the Salary Base cannot include (1) taxable benefits under section 6 of the ITA, (2) stock option benefits under section 7 of the ITA, (3) bonuses and remuneration based on profits, (4) inducement payments, (5) employer's share of related benefits, or (6) prior-year unpaid remuneration paid in the current taxation year (subsection 78(4), reported on Line 310 of Form T661).

Furthermore, under ITR subsection 2900(6), the PPA cannot exceed the Overall Cap on PPA, which ensures that total qualified SR&ED expenditures, the PPA, and specific statutory deductions do not exceed total business expenditures deducted in the year:
Overall Cap on PPA = A − B − C

where A is total amounts deducted when calculating net income for tax purposes from the business for the year (including cost of goods sold); B is the sum of deductions claimed in the year under sections 20 (CCA, interest, bad debts), 24 (ceasing business), 26 (banks), 30 (improving land for farming), 32 (insurance agents/brokers), 37 (Section 37 SR&ED pool deduction), 66 to 66.8 (exploration and development expenses), and 104 (trusts) of the Income Tax Act; and C is expenditures incurred for the use of, or the right to use, a building.
4. Unpaid Remuneration (Subsection 78(4)) and Foreign SR&ED Salaries (Subsections 37(1.4)–(1.5))

Under subsection 78(4) of the ITA, any SR&ED salary or wages incurred in a taxation year that are not paid within 180 days from the end of that taxation year are deemed not to have been incurred in that taxation year. When paid in a subsequent year, they are reported on Line 310 of Form T661 for the Section 37 pool and ITC, but are permanently excluded from the PPA Salary Base under ITR 2900(9).

Under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5), a claimant may claim permissible salary or wages for SR&ED work carried on outside Canada (reported on Line 307 for non-specified employees and Line 309 for specified employees), equal to the lesser of Amount A and Amount B:

items: Amount A: Total salary or wages for SR&ED work carried on outside Canada where (a) the work was directly undertaken by an employee of the claimant (not a contractor), (b) the employee was a resident of Canada at the time the expense was incurred, (c) the work related to a business of the claimant, (d) the work was an integral part and solely in support of SR&ED carried on in Canada by the claimant (dual-purpose work supporting non-SR&ED or foreign R&D is ineligible), and (e) the salary or wages were not subject to income or profits tax from another country.

Amount B (The 10% Limit): 10% of the total SR&ED salary or wages for SR&ED carried on in Canada (calculated by the CRA as 10% of Line 306 of Form T661). Under the Traditional Method, no SR&ED overhead or other expenditures (such as foreign travel, hotel, and meal costs) are allowed under subsection 37(1) in respect of work performed outside Canada, even if the employee's salary qualifies under subsection 37(1.4).

body.text: 5.3 Overhead and Other Expenditures Under the Traditional Method (ITR 2900(2)(c) & 2900(3))

Claimants electing the Traditional Method may claim overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 of Form T661 if the expenditure (or a reasonable allocated portion thereof) satisfies two cumulative statutory tests under paragraphs 2900(2)(c) and 2900(3)(b) of the Income Tax Regulations:

items: The "Directly Related" Test: The expenditure must connect directly—with no intervening step or intermediary—to (a) the SR&ED work, (b) the SR&ED staff, or (c) the machinery or equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED.
The "Incremental" Test: The expenditure would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada not occurred.

body.text: Under the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy, specific overhead items are treated as follows:

items: Employer's Share of Related Benefits: Employer contributions to related benefits for employees directly undertaking, supervising, or supporting SR&ED are allowable on Line 360 in proportion to their SR&ED work, whereas related benefits for administrative staff are disallowed due to an indirect link.

Selection, Hiring, and Relocation of SR&ED Personnel: Pre-employment costs—specifically (1) headhunter fees, (2) recruitment advertising expenses, (3) candidate selection travel costs, and (4) immigration, work permit, or visa costs—are disallowed for SR&ED (deductible only as regular business expenses) because they occur before the individual becomes an employee. Conversely, (5) moving expenses related to selected candidates or relocating SR&ED employees to another facility within Canada, and (6) related employee taxable benefits (such as covering a housing loss) are allowable in both the Section 37 pool and ITC base under the Traditional Method if directly related and incremental (provided the hired employee actually performs SR&ED work).

Training, Subscriptions, Utilities, Waste Disposal, and Retiring Allowances: Technological training in Canada required for an ongoing claimed SR&ED project, periodical subscriptions specifically related to the project's technology, incremental plant utilities (water, electricity, fuel), waste disposal costs where scrap material is directly recycled or used in an ongoing SR&ED project (normal waste disposal after SR&ED finishes is disallowed), and an incremental SR&ED-allocated portion of a retiring allowance are allowable on Line 360.

Prescribed Expenditures Discrepancy (ITR Section 2902(a)): Certain incremental expenditures—such as third-party professional fees paid to prepare SR&ED claims, technical conference/convention costs (ITR 2902(a)(i)(F)), and interest on borrowed money used for SR&ED (ITA s. 20(1)(c))—may be included in the Section 37 deductible pool under the Traditional Method, but are prescribed expenditures under Regulation 2902(a) that must be subtracted on Line 530 of Form T661 and cannot earn an ITC. (Internal employee salaries for preparing an SR&ED claim under the Traditional Method are excepted from Regulation 2902 under clause 2902(a)(i)(A) if directly related and incremental.)

body.text: 5.4 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed (Materials for SR&ED Policy)

Under both the Traditional Method (ITR paragraph 2900(2)(a)) and the Proxy Method (ITA subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V)), a claimant may claim on Line 320 of Form T661 the cost of materials consumed or materials transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. To qualify as "materials for SR&ED," the raw materials, substances, or items must be physical and tangible (in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) and must, at a given moment in the SR&ED process, compose the body of a tangible thing on which the SR&ED is being carried out or that results from the SR&ED.

Materials consumed are materials destroyed, absorbed, used up, or rendered virtually valueless (experimental production sold or valued at less than 10% of original cost) as a result of the prosecution of SR&ED. Materials transformed are materials that have not been rendered virtually valueless after SR&ED, but have been transformed in or as a result of the prosecution of SR&ED (such as components incorporated into a custom product, commercial asset, or experimental production run). If materials transformed are subsequently sold or converted to commercial use within 20 years, the ITC earned on those materials is subject to ITC Recapture under subsections 127(27) to 127(36).

Processing supplies and laboratory items that do not compose the body of the object being researched—such as petri dishes, beakers, flasks, pipettes, cleaning supplies, broken or used lab supplies, used lubricants such as engine oil, general utilities, CDs/DVDs, data, and software licences—do not qualify as materials for SR&ED. Furthermore, materials can only be claimed in the taxation year in which they are actually consumed or transformed in SR&ED (never when received from a supplier or merely removed from inventory) and must be paid within 180 days of tax year-end (subsection 127(26)). Cost means laid-down cost (invoice cost, customs and excise duties, transportation, and storage) or, for self-manufactured goods, industrial cost price (laid-down cost of materials, direct labour, and production overhead, even when using the Proxy Method). For materials purchased from a non-arm's length supplier, the ITC is restricted to the cost incurred by the non-arm's length supplier excluding any profit element (subsection 127(11.6)).
5.5 Subcontractor Expenditures (ITA s. 37(1)(a)(i.01)) and Third-Party Payments (ITA s. 37(1)(a)(i.1)–(iii))
1. Arm's-Length vs. Non-Arm's Length SR&ED Contracts

When a claimant contracts another party to perform SR&ED in Canada on behalf of the claimant (subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01)), the tax treatment depends on whether the contractor deals at arm's length with the claimant:

items: Arm's-Length SR&ED Contracts (Line 340): Provided the work is performed in Canada on behalf of the claimant by a taxable supplier (subsection 127(9)), 100% of the contract expenditure is deductible in the Section 37 pool, and 80% of the expenditure qualifies for the SR&ED ITC (a 20% reduction is applied on Line 529 of Form T661). Contract payments for work not yet performed are barred as prepaid expenses (subsection 18(9)), and amounts unpaid 180 days after year-end are excluded from qualified expenditures (subsection 127(26)) until the year paid (when 80% of the paid amount is added on Line 500). In addition, because capital expenditures were restored after December 15, 2024, contract expenditures and third-party payments incurred after December 15, 2024 generally are no longer reduced by related non-current performer expenditures under the former look-through rule (subsections 37(14) and 37(15)).

Non-Arm's Length (NAL) SR&ED Contracts (Line 345): Where the contractor does not deal at arm's length with the payer, the contract amount is 100% deductible in the payer's Section 37 pool, but 0% qualifies for an ITC in the payer's hands (paragraph 127(9)(f)). Instead, the NAL performer claims its own SR&ED expenditures and ITCs (even if contracted for support work only), and the payment received from the NAL payer does not reduce the NAL performer's qualified expenditures. Alternatively, under subsection 127(13), the NAL performer may transfer all or a portion of its qualified expenditures (up to the contract amount) to the NAL payer using Form T1146 (reported on Line 508 for the transferee and Line 546 for the transferor).

body.text: 2. Third-Party Payments (Third-Party Payments Policy & Form T1263)

body.text: 5.6 Restoration of SR&ED Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), Lease Costs, and Cloud/Bandwidth Rules (Post-December 15, 2024)
1. SR&ED Capital Expenditures (SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy, Updated June 29, 2026)

Effective for property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, capital expenditures are restored for both the Section 37 deductible pool (ITA paragraph 37(1)(b)) and the Section 127 ITC (ITA subsection 127(9)). To qualify as an SR&ED capital expenditure (reported on Line 390 and itemized in Part 6B, Box 782 and Lines 262–263 of Form T661), the expenditure must satisfy five requirements:

items: Depreciable Property Owned by Claimant: Must be depreciable property (ITA subsection 13(21)) owned by the claimant (or in which the claimant holds a leasehold interest, other than in a building or land) for which capital cost allowance (CCA) could otherwise be claimed under paragraph 20(1)(a). Non-depreciable assets such as land (ITR 1102(2)), inventory (ITR 1102(1)(b)), and goodwill/eligible capital property are excluded.

Statutory Exclusion of Buildings (ITA Paragraphs 37(8)(d) and (e)): Buildings and leasehold interests in buildings (including mobile homes with wheels removed and affixed to cement pads with utility hookups) are strictly excluded from both the Section 37 pool and ITCs, with the narrow exception of special-purpose buildings prescribed by Regulation 2903 (approved by the Department of Finance Canada on a building-by-building basis). Portable shelters and structures (such as bridges or transmission towers) are not restricted as buildings.

Post-December 15, 2024 Acquisition and Available-for-Use (ITA Subsection 37(1.2)): The property must be acquired after December 15, 2024 and cannot be claimed until the taxation year in which it becomes available for use.

The "All or Substantially All" (ASA ≥ 90%) Intent Test: At the time of acquisition, the claimant must intend either (a) that the property will be used during all or substantially all (90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life in the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada (ITA subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III) and (B)(III)), OR (b) that all or substantially all (90% or more) of its value will be consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada.

Crucial Distinction Between New and Used Capital Equipment (ITR Paragraph 2902(b)): New depreciable property qualifies for 100% immediate deduction in the Section 37 pool (Line 390) AND qualifies as a qualified expenditure for ITC purposes (earning 35% for CCPCs/ECPCs up to the $6M limit, with 40% cash refundability, or 15% above the limit). Conversely, used depreciable property (and refurbishment of used property) acquired after December 15, 2024 qualifies for the 100% Section 37 income deduction on Line 390, but is a prescribed expenditure under Regulation 2902(b) that must be subtracted on Line 532 of Form T661 and is ineligible to earn SR&ED ITCs. Any capital expenditure claimed on Line 390 of Form T661 must not be included on CCA Schedule T2SCH8.

body.text: 2. Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) (SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy, Updated May 22, 2026)

Where new machinery or equipment acquired after December 15, 2024 is used for both SR&ED and commercial manufacturing or processing—and therefore does not meet the 90% ASA test—it may qualify for partial ITCs as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) under subsection 127(9) (reported on Line 504 and Part 6C of Form T661). To qualify as SUE, the property must be (1) depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, (2) new property (never used, acquired to be used, or rented before acquisition), (3) not ASA (≥90%) SR&ED capital property, (4) not General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF), (5) not Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under Regulation 2900(11) (which disqualifies equipment intended at acquisition to be used for SR&ED during the assembly, construction, or commissioning of a commercial plant/line and intended over its expected useful life to be used primarily for non-SR&ED purposes), and (6) actually used primarily (more than 50% and less than 90% of its operating time) for SR&ED in Canada.
SUE is claimed across two periods:

items: First-Term SUE: Evaluated at the end of the first taxation year that occurs at least 12 months after the property was acquired and became available for use. If actual SR&ED operating time over that first period exceeded 50%, 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost of the equipment (without borrowed money costs under s. 21 and adjusted for NAL rules under s. 127(11.6)) is included as a qualified expenditure on Line 504 to earn an SR&ED ITC.

Second-Term SUE: Evaluated at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after the property was acquired and became available for use. If the property qualified as First-Term SUE and was used primarily (> 50%) for SR&ED during its operating time in the second period, an additional 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost is included as a qualified expenditure on Line 504. Unlike ASA capital expenditures, the capital cost of SUE is not part of the Section 37 deductible SR&ED pool; instead, the taxpayer depreciates the equipment under regular CCA rules on Schedule T2SCH8, and any SUE ITC applied or refunded reduces the Undepreciated Capital Cost (UCC) of the class in the subsequent taxation year.

body.text: 3. Equipment Lease Expenditures (SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy, Updated June 8, 2026) and Cloud/Bandwidth Rules

For lease payments incurred after December 15, 2024 (reported on Lines 350 and 355 and reconciled to Part 6A, Box 759 of Form T661), eligibility depends on the percentage of total operating time the leased equipment is used in SR&ED in Canada during the taxation year:

items: All or Substantially All (ASA ≥ 90% Operating Time): 100% of the lease cost is allowable in both the Section 37 pool and ITC base under the Traditional Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)) and the Proxy Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I), excluding GPOEF).

Primarily (> 50% to < 90% Operating Time): Under the Proxy Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI)), 50% of the cost to lease the equipment (other than GPOEF) may be claimed. Under the Traditional Method, the proportional percentage of SR&ED operating time may be claimed on Line 360 as overhead and other expenditures, provided it is directly related and incremental (ITR paragraph 2900(2)(c)).

50% or Less Operating Time (≤ 50%): Under the Proxy Method, 0% of the lease cost can be claimed. Under the Traditional Method, the proportional SR&ED percentage may be claimed on Line 360 as overhead if directly related and incremental.

Dedicated Bandwidth and Remote Compute (Data Kinetics Rule): Under Section 4.3.1 of the CRA's SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026), applying Data Kinetics Ltd. v. The Queen (98 DTC 1877), costs incurred after December 15, 2024 for dedicated bandwidth or leased access to a remote mainframe/equipment qualify as lease of equipment under the Proxy Method because bandwidth is made available through sophisticated optoelectronic equipment and is not a lease for General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF). Accounting guidance for SaaS startups likewise emphasizes maintaining separate cloud cost accounts for "production infrastructure" versus "development/R&D infrastructure," as only the dedicated R&D infrastructure is SR&ED-eligible.

body.text: 6. Government Assistance, Contract Payments, ITC Recapture, and Tax Treatment of Credits
6.1 Government Assistance, Non-Government Assistance, and Contract Payments (ITA s. 127(9), s. 127(18)–(20))

To prevent duplication of tax incentives, the Income Tax Act requires reductions for government assistance, non-government assistance, and contract payments that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing-due date for the taxation year:

items: Government Assistance (ITA Subsection 127(9)): Any grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, investment allowance, or other form of assistance from a government, municipality, Crown corporation, foreign government, or other public authority—other than the federal SR&ED ITC itself. Common examples include NRC-IRAP grants and all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits. As affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in CAE Inc. (2022 FCA), government loans related to SR&ED also constitute government assistance.

Non-Government Assistance (ITA Subsection 127(9) & Paragraph 12(1)(x)): Any inducement, reimbursement, contribution, or allowance received from a non-government entity for the cost of property or an outlay/expense that would be included in income under paragraph 12(1)(x).

Contract Payments (ITA Subsection 127(9)): An amount paid or payable to a claimant by a taxable supplier for SR&ED performed for or on behalf of an arm's-length person or partnership entitled to deduct the amount as a current SR&ED expenditure or third-party payment, or an amount for a current expenditure payable by a Canadian government, municipality, public authority, or Part I tax-exempt entity (section 149) for SR&ED to be performed for it or on its behalf. Whether a commercial contract constitutes a "contract payment" depends on contractor performance requirements, pricing versus risks assumed (ceiling price clauses or obligations to absorb cost overruns), IP rights, and whether the contract is for services or the sale of goods (Com Dev Ltd., 96-4343-IT-G · 1999).

body.text: Government and non-government assistance reduce both the Section 37 deductible pool (paragraph 37(1)(d), Lines 429–432 of Form T661) and qualified expenditures (subsection 127(9)), whereas contract payments reduce only the performer's qualified expenditures for ITC purposes and do not reduce the performer's Section 37 pool. Furthermore, the reduction of qualified expenditures is applied on a project-by-project basis (subsections 127(18) and 127(19)): excess assistance or contract payments on one project reduce that project's qualified expenditures to nil (and carry forward to reduce that same project in future years) without reducing unrelated projects. Among non-arm's length group members, assistance can be allocated using Form T1145 (subsection 127(20), Line 540 of Form T661).

body.text: 6.3 Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credits (Subsections 127(27) to 127(36))

Under subsections 127(27) through 127(36) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (updated October 14, 2022), if a claimant sells or converts to commercial use any property—specifically ASA capital equipment, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), or materials transformed (including experimental production or custom/commercial asset components)—within 20 taxation years of acquiring the property (subsection 127(36) extending the 10-year period in paragraph 127(27)(a) to 20 years), the claimant must add a recapture amount directly to its Part I tax payable for the year of disposition or conversion.

For corporations and individuals (where no Form T1146 transfer occurred), the amount added to Part I tax payable under subsection 127(27) is the lesser of (1) the SR&ED ITC originally earned in respect of the particular property, AND (2) the amount determined by multiplying the historical rate (35%, 15%, or 20% if earned prior to 2014) by either (a) the proceeds of disposition (paragraph 127(27)(b)) if disposed of to an arm's-length person, OR (b) the fair market value (FMV) of the property (paragraph 127(27)(c)) if converted to commercial use or disposed of to a non-arm's length party. Where qualified expenditures were transferred between non-arm's length parties under subsection 127(13) (Form T1146), subsection 127(29) requires the performer to add to Part I tax the lesser of the transferee's ITC on the transferred expenditure and (A × B) − C, where A is the percentage used by the transferee to determine its ITC, B is proceeds of disposition or FMV, and C is any recapture amount relating to the untransferred portion.

Recapture never applies to SR&ED salaries, overhead, or the sale/conversion of intellectual property (IP), nor does it apply under the de minimis rule if scrap sale proceeds or FMV at conversion are less than 10% of the total cost of the property. Under subsection 127(34), recapture does not apply when SR&ED capital property is disposed of to a non-arm's length purchaser that continues to use the property All or Substantially All (ASA ≥ 90%) for SR&ED. All amounts added to Part I tax payable under the recapture rules increase the claimant's Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in the following taxation year (paragraph 37(1)(c.2), reported on Line 453 of Form T661).

body.text: 7.2 Deep-Dive Analysis of Key Provincial Regimes
1. Quebec's Restructured CRIC Regime (Post-March 25, 2025) vs. Legacy R&D Credits

In the Quebec 2025–2026 Budget, the provincial government enacted a comprehensive overhaul of Quebec's innovation tax credits. Effective for taxation years (and partnership fiscal periods) beginning after March 25, 2025, Quebec abolished its legacy R&D credits—specifically eliminating the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) (Form RD-1029.7), the Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.6), the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research (Form RD-1029.8.16.1), the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.9.03), the Tax Credit for Technological Adaptation Services, and the Industrial Design Credit.

In their place, Quebec established the unified Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), administered by Revenu Québec using Form RD-222, Form RD-1029.8.CR, and Form RD-1029.8.PR. As detailed in provincial budget publications and legal commentaries, the CRIC regime introduces five major structural features:

items: Universal 30% / 20% Refundable Rate Structure: Every corporation carrying on business in Quebec earns a 100% refundable 30% tax credit on the first $1,000,000 of eligible expenditures above the exclusion threshold, and a 100% refundable 20% tax credit on all excess eligible expenditures, regardless of company size (corporations that are members of a qualified partnership earn a 20% rate).

Exclusion Threshold Formula: To qualify for CRIC, eligible expenditures must exceed an exclusion threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 OR the sum of the Basic Personal Amounts for R&D/pre-commercialization employees (for example, $18,751 per employee in 2025, prorated for time spent on eligible activities).

Coverage of Pre-Commercialization Activities: While core R&D eligibility remains harmonized with the federal SR&ED definition (with scientific reviews conducted by the CRA), CRIC expands eligible activities to include pre-commercialization work in Quebec connected to R&D: testing, technological validation, initial regulatory approval/certification studies, functional and aesthetic product design, and initial approval quality control.

Inclusion of Capital Expenditures: CRIC covers expenditures to acquire new depreciable capital property (such as lab equipment, machinery, and development servers) used in Quebec for R&D or pre-commercialization, excluding real estate property (land, buildings, and rights of use over buildings).

50% Subcontractor and University Rule: Unlike the federal 80% rule, CRIC includes 50% of payments made to arm's-length subcontractors, eligible universities, public research centres, and research consortia for work performed in Quebec. CRIC does not provide an overhead proxy (PPA).

body.text: 2. Ontario (OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC)
Ontario administers three distinct corporate R&D tax credits through the CRA on the T2 return:

items: Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC): An 8% fully refundable credit on up to $3,000,000 of qualified Ontario current expenditures (shared across an associated group). Unlike British Columbia, Ontario has not adopted the federal $6,000,000 limit or confirmed the addition of restored federal capital expenditures to the OITC base. The $3,000,000 OITC expenditure limit phases out when prior-year federal taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000, or when prior-year specified paid-up capital is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000.

Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — T2SCH508): A 3.5% non-refundable credit on eligible Ontario expenditures (after subtracting the OITC claimed: (Amount minus OITC) × 3.5%), with no expenditure cap. Unused ORDTCs may be carried back 3 years and carried forward 20 years.

Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC): A 20% fully refundable credit on qualified expenditures incurred under eligible R&D contracts with Eligible Research Institutes (ERIs) in Ontario, up to an annual expenditure cap of $20,000,000 per associated group.

body.text: 3. British Columbia (Express Federal Alignment and Permanent Status)

British Columbia expressly aligned its BC SR&ED Tax Credit (Form T666) with the federal Bill C-15 changes for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024: BC doubled the annual expenditure limit for its 10% refundable credit from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000, increased the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, extended the 10% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and restored capital expenditures as qualifying BC expenditures. Additionally, BC Budget 2026 removed the credit expiry date, making the BC provincial credit permanent. Qualifying BC expenditures not included in the refundable calculation earn a 10% non-refundable BC credit (carryback 3 years, carryforward 10 years). Form T666 must be filed within 18 months of the end of the taxation year.
4. Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG)

Administered via AT1 Schedule 29 and Form AT4970, the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) provides a two-tier 100% refundable benefit on up to $4,000,000 of annual eligible R&D expenditures carried out in Alberta: an 8% base payment on eligible spending up to the corporation's base level (calculated as the average of qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the two preceding years), and an enhanced 20% payment (8% base plus 12% incremental benefit) on eligible spending exceeding the two-year historical base level. Updated guidance published on June 30, 2026 confirmed the continued independent operation of the IEG under the $4,000,000 expenditure cap without adopting the federal $6,000,000 limit or wholesale capital expenditure restoration. The filing deadline for the Alberta IEG is 15 months after the corporation's filing-due date.
