body.text: 8.2 Statutory Reporting Deadlines and the Absolute Bar Against Late Filing (ITA s. 37(11), s. 127(9)(m), and s. 220(2.2))

Under subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m) of the Income Tax Act, a claimant's SR&ED reporting deadline is strictly 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred:

items: Corporations: Because a corporation's T2 filing-due date under paragraph 150(1)(a) is 6 months after its taxation year-end, the corporate SR&ED reporting deadline is 18 months after the end of the taxation year (for example, a tax year ended December 31, 2025 has a Form T661 deadline of June 30, 2027).

Individuals (Sole Proprietorships): Because an individual carrying on a business has a T1 filing-due date of June 15 of the following year, the SR&ED reporting deadline is 17.5 months after the end of the tax year.

Trusts: Because a trust's T3 filing-due date is within 90 days after its taxation year-end, the SR&ED reporting deadline is 90 days plus 12 months (generally up to 15 months) after the end of the taxation year.

Partnerships: Form T661 should be filed with the Partnership Information Return (Form T5013) no later than 12 months after the earliest of all filing-due dates for the income tax returns of the members for the tax year in which the partnership's fiscal period ends (and each partner must file Schedule 31 or Form T2038(IND) by their own reporting deadline).
Non-Profit SR&ED Corporations: The reporting deadline is the corporation's income tax return filing-due date, which is up to 6 months after the end of the tax year.

body.text: Pursuant to subsection 220(2.2) of the Income Tax Act (applicable on and after November 17, 2005), requests to waive filing requirements under subsection 220(2.1) cannot be made in respect of the SR&ED reporting deadline. If Form T661 or Schedule 31 / Form T2038(IND) containing the prescribed information is not filed on or before the reporting deadline, the expenditures are not considered to be SR&ED expenditures and the claimant does not earn the ITC.
8.3 Elective Pre-Claim Approval (Launched April 1, 2026), CRA Service Standards, and the Coordinated Review Process
1. Elective Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026)

On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval process allowing eligible businesses (with gross business income below $25,000,000) to determine whether planned projects qualify for SR&ED tax incentives before starting work or incurring costs. Applications are submitted via My Business Account, and the CRA provides technical determinations within eight weeks. When a claim containing only pre-claim approved projects is subsequently filed and selected for expenditure-only review, the CRA processes the review within 90 calendar days.
2. CRA Processing Service Standards

The CRA's processing service standards apply to refundable SR&ED claims (the CRA commits to meeting these standards 90% of the time, and in 2025–2026 met the 60-day standard 95% of the time; there is no service standard for non-refundable claims):

items: 60 Calendar Days: Refundable claims that are accepted as filed.
90 Calendar Days: Refundable claims selected for review that only include projects granted Pre-Claim Approval (expenditure-only review).
180 Calendar Days: Refundable claims selected for review that include any project not granted Pre-Claim Approval or that materially differs from what was granted Pre-Claim Approval.

body.text: 3. The Coordinated Technical and Financial Review Process

Once an SR&ED claim is selected for review (based on risk assessment or random sampling), the claimant cannot withdraw the claim, because Form T661 is part of the income tax return and the Part 10 certification cannot be revoked. First-time claimants (or claimants who have not submitted a claim in the last 3 years) may also be selected for the mandatory virtual First-Time Claimant Advisory Service (FTCAS).
For claims selected for review, the CRA conducts a Coordinated Review led jointly by two specialists:

items: Research and Technology Advisor (RTA): Evaluates the technical aspects of the claim to determine whether the work meets SR&ED eligibility requirements, reporting to a Research and Technology Manager (RTM). Under the Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors, the RTA interviews the personnel who performed and supervised the work, tours the premises (virtually or on-site), examines contemporaneous evidence declared on Lines 270–282 of Form T661, and must not negotiate eligibility or expenditures with the claimant.
Financial Reviewer (FR): Reviews the financial aspects to determine whether claimed expenditures are allowable, reporting to a Financial Review Manager (FRM).

body.text: Information requests in the CRA's initial letter generally carry a 30-day response deadline. At the conclusion of the review, if adjustments are proposed, the RTA and FR issue a coordinated Proposal Package (including the SR&ED Project Eligibility Report and a financial proposal letter), giving the claimant 30 days to respond.
8.4 Administrative Second Review (Form RC532), Formal Objections, Judicial Appeals, and Gross Negligence Penalties
1. Multi-Tier Dispute Resolution and Administrative Review (Form RC532)
Under the CRA's Guidelines for Resolving Claimants' SR&ED Concerns, if disagreements arise during a review before the file is closed, the claimant may follow three escalation steps:

items: Step 1: Discuss concerns directly with the assigned RTA and/or FR.
Step 2: Involve the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) and/or Financial Review Manager (FRM).

Step 3 — Request an Administrative Review (Form RC532): Before the 30-day proposal period expires and before the file is closed, the claimant may inform the reviewers and submit Form RC532 (Request for Administrative Review) to the National SR&ED Administrative Review Intake Centre (Canada Revenue Agency, Business Tax Incentives Directorate, Enterprise Building, 13th Floor, 427 Laurier Ave W, Ottawa ON K1A 0L5). Forwarded within 3 business days to the local SR&ED Assistant Director, the Administrative Review evaluates whether due process was granted and whether the technical and financial reviews complied with current SR&ED legislation and policies.

body.text: 2. Notice of Objection and Judicial Appeals
Once a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is issued, the claimant may pursue formal recourse:

items: CRA Appeals Branch — Notice of Objection (Form T400A or Form RC592): Must be filed within 90 days from the date of the Notice of Assessment or Reassessment (individuals other than trusts have until the later of 90 days after the notice or 1 year after the T1 filing-due date; extensions of up to 1 year may be requested). Large Corporations (total taxable capital employed in Canada by the corporation and related corporations exceeding $10,000,000) must explicitly describe each issue and specify the exact dollar relief sought, and must pay 50% of the disputed amount upfront.

Tax Court of Canada: Must receive the Notice of Appeal within 90 days of the CRA Appeals Branch's notice of confirmation or reassessment (or after 90 days have elapsed since filing the objection without a decision).

Federal Court of Appeal & Supreme Court of Canada: Appeals to the Federal Court of Appeal must be filed within 30 days of the Tax Court's final judgment (excluding July and August), and applications for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada must be filed within 60 days of the Federal Court of Appeal's judgment (excluding July).

body.text: 3. Gross Negligence Penalties on Overstated SR&ED Claims (ITA Subsection 163(2))

Under subsection 163(2) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025), if a claimant knowingly, or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence (such as claiming projects known not to involve SR&ED, describing fictitious or misdated activities, or continuing to claim disallowed, miscalculated, or unsubstantiated amounts after being advised in writing by the CRA), makes or participates in a false statement or omission, the penalty is the greater of $100 or 50% of:

items: the understated Part I tax payable reasonably attributable to the false statement or omission; plus
the refund of the overstated refundable ITC claimed by the claimant.

body.text: Under subsection 163(3), the CRA bears the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities to show that the false statement or omission resulted from more than a simple oversight or misunderstanding of the Act. However, when the gross negligence penalty applies to the refund of a refundable ITC (paragraph 163(2)(d)), the CRA calculates the 50% penalty on the entire overstated refund regardless of what caused individual portions of the overstatement, and under subsection 163(2.1), taxable income in a net loss year is deemed not to be less than zero.
9. Judicial Precedents and Canadian SR&ED Case Law Analysis (1988–2026)

Canadian SR&ED eligibility and financial compliance are shaped by decisions of the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA). The following analysis synthesizes the governing body of Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence from 1988 through 2026.
9.1 Foundational Appellate and Tax Court Precedents on the Meaning of SR&ED

items: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (TCC): The foundational judicial authority in Canadian SR&ED law. Justice Bowman set out the five criteria for SR&ED eligibility (technological risk or uncertainty not removable by routine engineering; formulation of hypotheses; procedures according with the scientific method; technological advancement; and detailed contemporaneous records kept as the work progressed) and established "system uncertainty" as a valid basis for eligibility.

Sass Manufacturing Limited v. M.N.R., 88 DTC 1363 (TCC): Judge Sarchuk defined "systematic investigation or search," establishing the repeatability and systematic observation requirements that distinguish SR&ED from trial-and-error adjustments.

RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087, 235 N.R. 258 (1998 FCA): The Federal Court of Appeal (Justice Robertson) endorsed Northwest Hydraulic and established that (a) failed research efforts qualify for SR&ED, as holding otherwise is "contrary to common sense and the goal of encouraging entrepreneurship"; (b) while adducing documentary evidence showing the logical progression between successive tests is the "only sure-fire way" of proving systematic research, a judge may infer systematic research where records were lost or where testing led to an actual technological advancement; and (c) whether work constitutes SR&ED is a question of law or mixed law and fact for the court, not expert witnesses, whose role is limited to "providing the court with a pair of prescription glasses through which technical information may be viewed".

C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393; Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 FCA 355; and R&D Pro-Innovation Inc. v. Canada, 2016 FCA 152: Successive Federal Court of Appeal rulings affirming that the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria govern all SR&ED determinations.
Rainbow Pipe Line Co., 96-4369-IT-G · 1999 (TCC): Confirmed that the rejection of a hypothesis is itself a technological advancement.

body.text: 9.2 Appellate Reaffirmation of the Scientific Method Post-2021 Guidelines (Kam-Press and National R&D)
In back-to-back appellate rulings, the Federal Court of Appeal rejected arguments that the "scientific method" is not required under subsection 248(1) or was removed by the CRA's 2021 guidelines:

items: Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88 (aff'g 2019 TCC 246): Justice Webb dismissed the taxpayer's argument that the absence of the words "scientific method" in subsection 248(1) invalidated the third Northwest Hydraulic criterion, holding that under a textual, contextual, and purposive analysis (Canada Trustco, 2005 SCC 54), Northwest Hydraulic is the settled judicial interpretation of subsection 248(1).

National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 (aff'g 2020 TCC 47): Justice Rennie held that (1) the Northwest Hydraulic test is mandatory binding law rather than mere guidance, (2) the CRA's 2021 eligibility guidelines did not remove the requirement to follow the scientific method, (3) vague or unclear records that do not reflect a logical progression between the premise of an experiment and the result fail to establish SR&ED, and (4) expert witness reports that opine on the legal question of whether work constitutes SR&ED are inadmissible.

body.text: 9.3 Contemporary Case Law on Software, System Uncertainty, Manufacturing, and Penalties (2015–2026)

The table below summarizes key Tax Court of Canada and Federal Court of Appeal decisions from 2015 through 2026 across software engineering, industrial manufacturing, food science, financial compliance, and fraud penalties.

cells: Software & Industrial Control (SIL 4 train-control box vs. SCADA upgrade)

MTCLM project allowed: Cumulative "system uncertainty" in safety-critical SIL 4 train control could not be resolved by available methods. SCADACOM-5 project disallowed ($1,293,692): Modernization and scale-up with known tools is product development, not experimental development.
Software / Cloud SaaS (React & Redux integration performance)

Recognized systemic uncertainty in open-source tool integration (React/Redux) beyond routine debugging/optimization; encouraged holistic evaluation of software projects supported by metrics and testimony.
Food Processing (13 projects claimed across 2005–2009; wage estimation)
All 13 projects disallowed: no proven technological uncertainty or systematic hypothesis testing with records; wages estimated and split evenly across batches failed substantiation.
Manufacturing (Industrial heating elements; statute-barred years; s. 163(2) / s. 160)

Certain 2007–2008 heating element projects allowed, but 2006 & 2009 denied; plagiarized supplier/website text in technical reports was a misrepresentation that reopened statute-barred tax years and supported penalties.
Vortex Energy Services Ltd. v. The King 2025 TCC 63
Energy / Engineering (Mobile direct-contact fracking water heaters)
Prototyping was trial-and-error with vague/general hypotheses and lack of systematic test documentation or expert evidence.
Novel High-Pressure Processing (HPP) application for microbial stability qualified; hypotheses were tested via measurable observations (pH, microbial counts).
Paveit Construction Inc. v. The King 2025 TCC
Field adjustments were trial-and-error involving known variables with no technological advancement and poor records.
Buhler Versatile Inc. v. The King 2023 TCC 18
Heavy Manufacturing (Tractor design and subsystem integration)
Demonstrated how system integration uncertainties in complex machinery design satisfy the Northwest Hydraulic criteria.
Allegro Wireless Canada Inc. v. The Queen 2021 TCC 27
Software / Telecom / AI (3 wireless software projects)
Government loans related to SR&ED constitute government assistance that reduces qualified SR&ED expenditures.
Andre Lamy Medicine Professional Corp. v. The Queen 2020 TCC 61
Medical / Clinical Research (Directly engaged & on behalf of MPC)
Work by physician deemed performed on behalf of the Medical Professional Corporation across 4 eligible projects.
Upheld system uncertainty in precision machining, supported by favourable expert testimony.
Strictly enforced the 18-month statutory deadline: where projects were filed only by a related company, the claimant's incomplete filing was barred.
Easy Way Cattle Oilers Ltd. 2016 FCA (aff'g 2015 TCC 211)
Failure to file prescribed Schedule 31 containing all prescribed information within the statutory deadline bars the taxpayer from earning SR&ED ITCs.
Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen 2017 TCC 6
Addressed evidentiary standards and technological uncertainty in custom mechanical rigging systems.
Cross-disciplinary, industry-unique method satisfied all five Northwest Hydraulic criteria.
Strong evidence of technical uncertainty and technological advancement on printer design problems post-commercial sale.
Zeuter Development Corporation v. The Queen 2006 TCC 597, 2007 DTC 41
Confirmed that the claimant bears the burden of demonstrating with objective evidence that all SR&ED criteria were met.
